tasks.description: Use the `urllib.request` module (built-in) to fetch data from 'https://httpbin.org/get'. Print the status code.
tasks.hint:
`import urllib.request`
`with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response: print(response.status)`
Status 200 means OK. This is the built-in way — no extra install needed.
tasks.solution:
import urllib.request

url = 'https://httpbin.org/get'
with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response:
    print(response.status)
tasks.walkthrough:
`urlopen` sends a GET request and returns a response you can use in a `with` block, like a file.
`.status` is the HTTP status code; 200 means the request succeeded.

tasks.description: Fetch JSON from 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1'. Parse and print the 'title' field.
tasks.hint:
`import json, urllib.request`
`with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as r: data = json.loads(r.read())`
Then `print(data['title'])` — `json.loads()` converts the JSON bytes to a dict.
tasks.solution:
import json
import urllib.request

url = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1'
with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response:
    data = json.loads(response.read())

print(data['title'])
tasks.walkthrough:
`response.read()` gives the raw bytes of the body. `json.loads` parses them into a dictionary.
After that it's ordinary dictionary access to get the title field.

tasks.description: Install and use the `requests` library to fetch the same URL. Compare how much simpler it is.
tasks.hint:
Install: `pip install requests` in your terminal first.
`import requests; r = requests.get(url)`
`r.json()` automatically parses JSON — much cleaner than urllib!
`r.status_code` gives the HTTP status.
tasks.solution:
import requests

url = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1'
r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)

print(r.status_code)
print(r.json()['title'])
tasks.walkthrough:
With requests, the fetch is one line and `.json()` handles the decoding.
Compare with the previous task: no `with`, no `read()`, no `json.loads`.
Remember to `pip install requests` in a terminal first if you see ModuleNotFoundError.

tasks.description: Use `requests.get()` with query parameters to search. Pass `params={'q': 'python'}` to a test URL.
tasks.hint:
`requests.get(url, params={'key': 'value'})` appends `?key=value` to the URL.
`r.url` shows the full URL with parameters appended.
This is safer than manually building URL strings.
tasks.solution:
import requests

r = requests.get('https://httpbin.org/get', params={'q': 'python'}, timeout=10)

print(r.url)
print(r.json()['args'])
tasks.walkthrough:
The `params` dictionary becomes `?q=python` on the end of the URL, properly encoded.
httpbin echoes the query back under 'args', which confirms what the server received.

tasks.description: Handle a failed request gracefully: try fetching a URL that doesn't exist, catch the exception, and print a user-friendly error.
tasks.hint:
`requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` — raised when the server can't be reached.
`requests.exceptions.Timeout` — raised when the request times out.
`requests.get(url, timeout=5)` sets a 5-second timeout.
tasks.walkthrough:
The specific exceptions come first so each failure gets a tailored message.
`RequestException` at the end is the parent of all requests errors and catches anything else.
The `timeout` argument makes sure a silent server can't hang the program.

lesson.intro:
Most interesting data lives on the other side of an HTTP request. Python can
fetch it with the built-in `urllib`, or more comfortably with the `requests`
library. Today needs an internet connection, and for the later tasks the
`requests` package installed with pip.

If you're offline, read through the examples and solutions; the code is short
and the shape is what matters.

sections.heading: urllib: built in, a bit clunky
sections.body:
`urlopen` returns a response object. `.status` is the HTTP status code
(200 means OK). `.read()` gives the body as bytes, which you decode to
text or hand straight to `json.loads`.
sections.code:
import urllib.request
import json

url = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1'
with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response:
    print(response.status)
    data = json.loads(response.read())
print(data['title'])

sections.heading: requests: the usual choice
sections.body:
Install once from a terminal: `pip install requests`. Then `requests.get`
does the request, `.status_code` is the status, `.json()` parses the body.
Much shorter.

sections.heading: Query parameters
sections.body:
Pass `params=` as a dictionary and requests builds the `?key=value` part
of the URL for you, with proper escaping. `r.url` shows the final URL.
sections.code:
import requests

r = requests.get('https://httpbin.org/get', params={'q': 'python', 'page': 2})
print(r.url)
print(r.json()['args'])

sections.heading: When it fails
sections.body:
Networks fail. Wrap requests in `try` and catch the exceptions the library
raises: `ConnectionError` when the host can't be reached, `Timeout` when
it's too slow. Always pass a `timeout`, or a dead server can hang your
program forever.

watch_out: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'` means it isn't installed. Run `pip install requests` in a terminal, then try again.
`response.read()` from urllib is bytes, not a string. `json.loads` accepts bytes; `print` will show `b'...'`.
A status of 200 means success. 404 means not found, 500 means the server had a problem.
